power.title: Power Analysis Check
report:
::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

text.text: The underlying causes of contractile dysfunction in adenomyosis remain poorly understood.
In vivo cine MRI / TVUS captures contraction direction, velocity, and coordination, but does not have access to force or pressure.
Conversely, ex vivo strip studies report force but obliterate wavelike aspects of contraction propagation.
In vivo, uterine contractility is found to be restricted to the inner myometrium, which encompasses the JZ (5, (9) (10) (11).

text.text: It is not known whether the JZ or the inner myometrium exhibit distinct contractile features ex vivo, in an organ bath.

To address these questions and methodological gaps, we developed here an optical, ex vivo approach to measure contractile wave origin, amplitude, velocity, direction, and frequency across the entire myometrial thickness, from serosa to endometrium.
Our method draws on tissue displacement mapping techniques previously applied to intestinal smooth muscle (29, 30), and on speckle-tracking methods used in in vivo uterine studies (31).

text.text: Ethical approval for the study was granted by the Groupe Ethique Recherche Médicale (GERM) under approval number IRB 00012157.
All patients were provided with written information about the study and consented to participate.
Two adjacent full-thickness biopsies (~30 × 10 × 10 mm, serosa to endometrium) were cut out from the anterior wall, midway between cervix and fundus, avoiding any visible myomas.
The first biopsy was immediately fixed in 4% PFA overnight for immunofluorescence (n = 10 adenomyosis, n = 9 controls).
The second biopsy was transported in ice-cold medium (DMEM:F-12 + GlutaMAX, Gibco, Thermo Fisher) pre-oxygenated with carbogen (95% O2, 5% CO2).
Ex vivo contractility assays were performed on this second biopsy, within 6 hours of retrieval (n = 11 adenomyosis, n = 8 controls).
Ten patients (5 per group) contributed to both ex vivo contractility and immunofluorescence analysis.
Each fresh biopsy was further sliced into three ~1 mm thick strips (final size ~30 × 10 × 1 mm), with circumferential fibers running along the strip width.

Carbon black microparticles were adhered to each slice to serve as fiducial markers, and the 3 strips were pinned vertically (serosa at the top, endometrium at the bottom), next to each other, in a Sylgard-lined container at 37°C, continuously bubbled with carbogen (Figure 1A,C, Video S1).

text.text: Once spontaneous phasic contractions appeared (after 1-3 h), they were recorded at 1 frame per second (1Hz) with a Basler acA3800 camera mounted with a 25mm lens.
Recording times were 20 min for baseline and 30 min after 10 µM oxytocin (Sigma O4375) administration.
For each patient, contractile behaviour was averaged over all contractions in the recording intervals and over the three strips, thus reducing intra-patient technical variability.
We tracked displacement of carbon black particles adhered to the myometrium with the TrackV2 ImageJ plugin.
Three pairs of particles were selected for each strip, at the sub-serosal, midmyometrial, and sub-endometrial levels (Figure 1C).

text.text: For each pair, we computed the deformation relative to the relaxed state: 𝐷𝑒𝑓𝑜𝑟𝑚𝑎𝑡𝑖𝑜𝑛 (𝑡)(%) = 100 𝐷(𝑡)-𝐷 𝑟𝑒𝑙𝑎𝑥 𝐷 𝑟𝑒𝑙𝑎𝑥 , where D(t) is the inter-point distance (along x, i.e. perpendicular to the serosa-endometrium axis), and 𝐷 𝑟𝑒𝑙𝑎𝑥 the maximum interpoint-distance reached during the recording.

Traces were smoothed with a Gaussian filter (σ = 3 s), and contractions were detected using custom MATLAB peak-detection algorithms (https://github.com/emiliehuon/uterus_analysis_contractility), adjusting the minimum peak prominence for each recording (0.1 -1 %) to exclude noise.

text.text: We computed the frequency (peaks per 10 min), amplitude (peak-to-preceding valley, %), and duration (width at half-prominence, min).
For each propagating wave, its site of origin was measured directly from the video and normalised to strip length.
Velocity was measured as the distance travelled by the contractile wave divided by the travel time.
Sites of origin and velocity were averaged over all visible waves for each strip, and then over the three strips for each patient.
Other contraction parameters were averaged over the three pairs of points, and over the three strips (i.e., 9 measurements per patient).
The fixed biopsy was cryoprotected in 30% sucrose, embedded in PolyFreeze (Sigma), and cut in 18 µm sections deposited on Superfrost glass slides.

Slides were permeabilized and blocked in PBS, 1% BSA, and 0.1% Triton for 1 h, incubated overnight with Oxytocin receptor antibody (OTR, LS-A246, LSBio, 1:100), thoroughly washed, and further incubated in Alexa Fluor 647 anti-rabbit IgG (Thermo Fisher, 1:400, 3 h).
Slides were kept under gentle agitation throughout to optimize staining homogeneity.

They were finally washed, cover-slipped, and imaged at 10x on a Zeiss wide-field epifluorescence microscope (ImagoSeine platform), in mosaic mode to capture the full fluorescence distribution from serosa to endometrium.
Mosaic tiles (~100-200 per sample) were stitched with ZEN software (Zeiss).

text.text: Most uterine contractility organ bath studies focus on the force signal, without looking at the strip itself.
In this study, we harnessed optical tracking techniques commonly used in the assessment of intestinal motility to monitor the contractility of full-thickness myometrium strips.
This revealed key spatiotemporal -as opposed to just temporal -information about myometrial contractility.
This approach allowed us to compare outer vs inner myometrium and to derive data pertaining to contractile wave initiation and propagation.
The baseline ex vivo frequencies we find (~2 cycles / 10 min) are similar to ex vivo values reported with force transducers (33, 39), but are ~5-10 times lower than in vivo values (10, 17, 18).

text.text: How do we reconcile these apparently contradictory in vivo and ex vivo observations?
We have previously shown that ex vivo uterine contractility is insensitive to tetrodotoxin (41), i.e., it is myogenic.

Although nerve fibers are still present in the tissue we monitor, they have been severed from their nerve cell bodies in the hypogastric plexus (42) during the hysterectomy operation and are de facto no longer functional.

In a forthcoming publication, we show that adrenergic inhibitory innervation is mostly concentrated in the outer myometrium: it is reasonable to conclude that this innervation actively quenches, in vivo, the potential myogenic contractility of the outer myometrium.
At baseline, contractile waves originated at various sites along the myometrium thickness, either in the outer or the inner myometrium.

After oxytocin administration, contractile waves systematically originated in the inner myometrium (close to the endometrium) in both patient groups (Figure 2), and thereafter propagated to the outer myometrium.

It is known that oxytocin injection modulates the frequency and direction of uterine peristalsis in vivo (6, 18), and that OTR expression fluctuates across the menstrual cycle (43).

text.text: Their measurements were restricted to the outer myometrium of patients with highly symptomatic adenomyosis, whereas we averaged contractility over the whole myometrial thickness in a cohort that was not selected based on symptom severity.

Our results indicate that the spontaneous myogenic contractility of adenomyosis myometrium does not significantly differ from that of controls: our experiment does not capture alterations of the neurogenic component, which are, as we will show in a forthcoming publication, substantial.
We found that OTR density was ~2 times higher in adenomyosis than in controls (Figure 3), in agreement with previous reports of OTR overexpression in adenomyotic myometrium (27, 32).

text.text: Administration of 10 µM oxytocin increased contraction frequency in both patient groups.

The frequency increase was, however, not correlated with OTR expression: it was 1.6-fold lower in adenomyosis uteri than in controls, whereas OTR density was 1.8 times-fold higher in adenomyosis patients than in controls.
It is likely that the concentration we used (10 µM) is saturating, i.e., it yielded a response independent of OTR expression.
Dose-response experiments could reveal a sensitivity to lower oxytocin concentrations in adenomyosis uteri.
It is also possible that receptor overexpression does not translate to a stronger response if receptors are desensitised or internalised, or if downstream signalling is altered (33, 34).

text.text: Several limitations of this study should be acknowledged.
First, our sample size was modest (n = 8-11 per group), which limited statistical power: smaller between-group differences in oxytocininduced contractility may have gone undetected.
Many novel results were, however, common to both groups and therefore based on a more substantial number of patients (n = 19 total).
Second, we extracted contractile signals from operator-defined pairs of points: a more sophisticated approach would consider the full deformation field of the slice (31).
text.formatted: Second, we extracted contractile signals from operator-defined pairs of points: a more sophisticated approach would consider the full deformation field of the slice <ref type="bibr" target="#b30">(31)</ref>.

text.text: Third, we used a single oxytocin concentration and did not obtain full dose-response curves for adenomyosis vs control tissue.
These data will be provided in a future report.
The high concentration used (10 µM) appeared necessary to elicit changes in contractility in the non-pregnant, hysterectomy myometrium we examined.
The literature confirms that non-pregnant myometrium is much less sensitive to oxytocin than pregnant caesarean-section tissue (33, 37, 38).
text.formatted: The literature confirms that non-pregnant myometrium is much less sensitive to oxytocin than pregnant caesarean-section tissue <ref type="bibr" target="#b32">(33,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b36">37,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b37">38)</ref>.

text.text: Fourth, most of the adenomyosis tissue we collected did not present with adenomyosis lesions in the particular biopsy we retrieved; our data therefore pertains to potential systemic (myometrium-wide) alterations to myogenic contractility, rather than local alterations induced specifically by lesions.
We provided spatially resolved measurements of contractility across the whole thickness of the non-pregnant human myometrium, from serosa to endometrium.
Ex vivo contractility is purely myogenic, and myogenic motility was similar in the outer, middle, and inner myometrium.
This sharply contrasts with the in vivo (MRI, TVUS) observation that only the inner myometrium is involved in contractile activity.
We suggest that the difference resides in the neuro-myogenic activity of the uterus in vivo, i.e., active quenching of contractions by inhibitory nerve activity.
Oxytocin (10 µM) caused contractile waves to originate in the inner myometrium close to the endometrium, in a region where OTR density was highest.
This indicates that OTR spatial heterogeneity in the uterus can control the direction of uterine contractile waves during the menstrual cycle.
Although adenomyosis uteri exhibited higher OTR expression, their spontaneous and oxytocin-induced myogenic contractile behaviour did not differ substantially from that of control samples.

Figure 1.
Uterine contractile waves propagate with uniform amplitude across the whole myometrial thickness.
(A) Experimental setup.

Three full-thickness strips per patient are pinned vertically in an organ bath (1), thermoregulated at 37°C (2), continuously bubbled with carbogen (3), and recorded with a video camera (4) at 1 Hz for up to an hour.
(B) Representative 20-min kymograph showing three serosa-to-endometrium waves (arrows).
(C) A strip covered with carbon black particles for displacement tracking (still shot from Video S1).
Shown in red are the successive positions of three pairs of points (at the sub-serosa, mid-myometrium, and sub-endometrium), tracked over 20 min.
(D) Representative deformation traces of the three pairs of points at the sub-serosa (blue), mid-myometrium (orange), and sub-endometrium (yellow).
Frequency was derived from detected peaks (○), amplitude as peak-to-preceding-valley (▽) difference, and duration as width at half-prominence (-).
(E) Contraction amplitude at different positions along the myometrium, for all patients (n = 19: 11 adenomyosis, 8 controls).
Each point is the mean of three slices per patient (~5 contractions per slice per recording).
Repeated-measures one-way ANOVA with Tukey's post-hoc test; **p = 0.0048.
Figure 2.
Effects of oxytocin on the contractility of control and adenomyosis myometrium.
(A-F) Contractile parameters before and 7-30 min after oxytocin, in controls (blue, n = 8) and adenomyosis (red, n = 11); open boxes before oxytocin, filled boxes after oxytocin.
Each point represents one patient (mean of 5.0 ±1.8 contractions per strip, and for three strips per patient).
Two-way ANOVA (group x period, repeated measures on period), mixed-effects model, followed by Sidak's post-hoc test.
Comparisons not indicated were not significant.
(E, F) The sites of origin of the contractile waves are shown for all patients, with adenomyosis patients separated from controls.
(G) Representative kymograph of a myometrial strip along the serosa-to-endometrium axis, showing contraction frequency and direction change after administration of 10 µM oxytocin.
Figure 3: Oxytocin receptor density follows an increasing serosa-to-endometrium gradient and is higher in adenomyosis patients.
(A) Full-thickness myometrium section immunostained for OTR, mosaic of ~200 stitched tiles.
(B) Magnified view of one ROI used for analysis (780 x 780 µm; black square in A).
(C) Magnified view of the raw signal (blue square in B).
(D) Binary obtained by thresholding the Trainable Weka Segmentation probability map in Fiji.
(E) OTR density profiles ± SD along the serosa-to-endometrium axis (0 = serosa |1 = endometrium).
(F) Integrated OTR density (area under each profile) for adenomyosis (n = 10) and controls (n = 9).
Violin plots with median and quartiles; Welch's t-test, **p = 0.0015.
